principles.name: Innovation
principles.description: Invent what the world does not yet have: dream big, start small, take risks and learn fast, reasoning from first principles rather than copying existing models.
evidence_signals: Reasons from first principles (hardware limits, physics, math) instead of copying what others do
Describes a new approach the candidate originated and how it was proven
Starts with a small, cheap experiment to test a bold idea before scaling it

principles.name: Intellectual Honesty
principles.description: Seek the truth, know your real capabilities, acknowledge weaknesses openly, and learn from mistakes.
evidence_signals: Says plainly 'I don't know' or 'I was wrong' and explains how they found out
Reports bad news or a failed result early instead of hiding it
Separates measured facts from assumptions when explaining results

principles.name: Speed and Agility
principles.description: Stay alert, keep learning, and change course quickly when reality changes, so products ship at high speed.
evidence_signals: Describes changing a plan quickly after new data and the result
Shows fast iteration loops, for example prototypes or parallel experiments

principles.name: Excellence and Determination
principles.description: Hold the highest standards and measure work against what is physically possible (the 'speed of light' benchmark for both performance and schedules), not against competitors.
evidence_signals: Compares achieved performance with the theoretical limit, for example bandwidth or compute peak
Persists through a very hard technical problem and explains the steps

principles.name: One Team
principles.description: Share information openly and work as one integrated team across hardware, software and research; project teams form around skills, not reporting lines or politics.
evidence_signals: Gives an example of working across the hardware and software boundary or with another org
Shares knowledge and credit and helps other teams succeed
Influences people they do not manage by sharing data and context openly

rounds.name: Recruiter call
rounds.notes: Background and logistics; sometimes skipped for referrals. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical phone screen
rounds.notes: Coding, often in C or C++ (NVIDIA says technical candidates may get a coding exercise, usually on HackerRank), under time pressure. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager call
rounds.notes: Past work and fit with the team's domain; not always included before the onsite.

rounds.name: Onsite coding
rounds.notes: Usually two coding rounds, often systems-flavored (memory, concurrency, bit manipulation) or debugging existing code. NVIDIA requires an onsite, in-person interview before an offer; interviews are 30 to 60 minutes, one-on-one, small group or panel. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: Classic distributed design or GPU/CPU architecture design, tailored to the team.

rounds.name: Domain technical deep dive
rounds.notes: Team-specific concepts such as CUDA, GPU memory, operating systems, compilers, or LLM internals; may mix explanation with coding.

rounds.name: Hiring manager onsite
rounds.notes: Behavioral and project deep dive; disagreements, feedback, and motivation. Each panelist scores the candidate and a weak round usually ends the process.

rounds.name: Recruiter call
rounds.notes: ML background, projects or publications, and which team the candidate matches into. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical phone screen
rounds.notes: Python or PyTorch coding; for LLM teams it can be fully LLM-focused (decoding, KV cache, beam search). Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Deep learning fundamentals
rounds.interviewer_role: Senior deep learning engineer or researcher
rounds.notes: Transformers, training optimization, parallel training, quantization, and how models map onto GPU compute and memory.

rounds.name: ML coding from first principles
rounds.notes: Implement layers or algorithms such as softmax, attention, dropout or batch norm without library shortcuts. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: ML systems design
rounds.notes: Inference serving, batching, distributed training or GPU cluster design, with throughput and latency targets.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: Project deep dive, recent model trends, bridging research and engineering, and team fit.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, motivation and culture fit.

rounds.name: Product sense screen
rounds.notes: Problem definition, trade-offs and execution, often anchored in past work.

rounds.name: Technical depth
rounds.notes: GPU, CUDA and AI concepts and hardware/software trade-offs; depth depends on the team.

rounds.name: Product case presentation
rounds.interviewer_role: Panel of PMs and engineering leaders
rounds.notes: Reported by some candidates: a product challenge sent ahead, presented in about 30 minutes, then questions. Not in every loop.

rounds.name: Onsite product and strategy
rounds.notes: Product improvement, market opportunity, prioritization and metrics.

rounds.name: Hiring manager and cross-functional
rounds.notes: Products led end to end and cross-functional challenges.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Program background, technical depth and product-area interest. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager screen
rounds.notes: Mostly behavioral and program mechanics: prioritization, KPIs, conflict, with light technical probing.

rounds.name: Technical program depth
rounds.notes: Hardware and software development lifecycle, chip or software release milestones, and the team's domain (AI software, silicon, data center).

rounds.name: Program case study
rounds.notes: A program at risk or a hardware/software co-development schedule; some loops ask for a presentation of a past program.

rounds.name: Cross-functional and behavioral
rounds.interviewer_role: TPM peer or partner engineering manager
rounds.notes: Influence without authority, unblocking teams across geographies, and decisions that were not well received.

rounds.name: Director or VP
rounds.notes: Reported for senior roles: strategic thinking, leadership approach and fit.

rounds.name: Recruiter or hiring manager screen
rounds.notes: Solutions architect loop. Resume walkthrough, customer-facing and technical background, and motivation.

rounds.name: Technical screen
rounds.notes: Deep learning, GPU computing and system architecture; parallel programming or inference optimization questions are reported.

rounds.name: Customer scenario presentation
rounds.interviewer_role: Panel of solutions architects and sales leaders
rounds.notes: About 30 minutes presenting an AI infrastructure design for a given customer scenario, then questions.

rounds.name: NVIDIA platform deep dive
rounds.notes: DGX and HGX systems, NVLink versus InfiniBand, cluster design and troubleshooting low GPU utilization.

rounds.name: Customer engagement and behavioral
rounds.notes: Difficult customers, saying no, influencing product teams with customer feedback. Even leadership conversations are technical.

question_patterns.pattern: A time the candidate disagreed with a manager or senior engineer on a technical call, and how it was settled
The most challenging technical problem the candidate solved, the dead ends, and how they persisted
Feedback or a mistake the candidate had to face openly, and what changed
A time new information forced the candidate to change plans quickly
Walk through a project from the resume in depth, including low-level technical details and the candidate's own decisions
Why NVIDIA and why this team's domain (GPU software, AI infrastructure, drivers, and so on)
Explain a GPU programming concept and how it affects performance, and reason about the theoretical limit
Explain an operating system or memory concept and its cost in real systems
Design a service or low-level component (scheduler, allocator, inference service) and defend trade-offs
Explain a modern deep learning technique and why it matters for compute or memory
Improve an NVIDIA product for a user segment and define success metrics
Size and evaluate a market opportunity for NVIDIA technology and recommend a move
Choose between competing product investments with limited resources and explain the trade-offs
A time the candidate aligned teams they did not manage, often across hardware, software or geographies, to keep work moving
Explain how a model component or training technique works step by step, then what limits its speed or memory on a GPU
Design or tune a model serving path for a throughput and latency target and explain each optimization
A hardware or software program is slipping a milestone; diagnose the cause, choose trade-offs and decide what to tell leadership
Propose GPU infrastructure for a customer's AI workload, sizing it and justifying system and network choices

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager or someone more senior about a technical decision.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real technical disagreement. Explain both positions and the evidence you brought, such as a benchmark or prototype, rather than opinion. Show you raised it directly and respectfully, and that you would change your mind if the data said so. NVIDIA prizes intellectual honesty, so say clearly if you turned out to be wrong. End with the outcome and the working relationship. Pitfall: a story about personalities with no technical substance.

looking_for: Whether you argue technical points with evidence
Whether you change your mind when the data says so
strong_signals: Explains both positions and the data you brought
Raised it directly and respectfully
Admits it plainly if you turned out to be wrong
watch_outs: A personality clash with no technical substance
Opinion with no benchmark or prototype behind it

sample_questions.question: Describe the most challenging technical problem you have worked on and how you solved it.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Choose a problem with real depth, such as a performance, concurrency or hardware-related bug. Explain why it was hard, the hypotheses you tested, the tools you used (profilers, debuggers, counters), and dead ends. Quantify the result and, if possible, compare it with the theoretical best. Interviewers will drill into low-level details, so choose something you know thoroughly. Pitfall: a broad project summary with no technical specifics.

looking_for: The depth of your technical problem solving
How you form and test hypotheses
strong_signals: Explains why the problem was hard and the dead ends
Names the tools used, such as profilers or debuggers
Quantifies the result against a sensible baseline
watch_outs: A broad project summary with no technical specifics
Picking a problem you cannot explain in low-level detail

sample_questions.question: How do you deal with negative feedback? Give an example.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give a concrete case: the feedback, who gave it, your first reaction, and the specific changes you made. Show you treat feedback as information about reality, which is how NVIDIA frames intellectual honesty. Mention how you checked that the change worked. Pitfall: defensive framing or a trivial example.

looking_for: Whether you treat feedback as useful information
How you act on criticism
strong_signals: A concrete case with your honest first reaction
Specific changes and how you checked they worked
watch_outs: Defensive framing
A trivial example with nothing at stake

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a conflict on a team you were part of and how it was resolved.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the conflict and the stakes briefly, then your actions: understanding each side, getting facts, proposing a decision rule, and keeping information open. Show a one-team mindset across hardware, software or research groups when possible. Close with the result and what you would do differently. Pitfall: taking all the credit or blaming others.

looking_for: How you help resolve conflict on a team
Whether you work as one team across groups
strong_signals: Understands each side and gets the facts
Proposes a decision rule and keeps information open
Closes with the result and what you would change
watch_outs: Taking all the credit
Blaming others for the conflict

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a hard decision you had to make with limited information.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain the situation, what was unknown, and the cost of waiting. Show how you gathered the most important facts quickly, made a call you could revisit, and set signals to check it. Be honest about the outcome, including what you got wrong. NVIDIA values speed with honesty, so show both. Pitfall: a decision that was not actually hard.

looking_for: How you decide when information is incomplete
Whether you balance speed with honesty
strong_signals: Explains what was unknown and the cost of waiting
Makes a call you could revisit, with signals to check it
Honest about what you got wrong
watch_outs: A decision that was not actually hard
Waiting until the answer was obvious

sample_questions.question: Why NVIDIA, and why this team in particular?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Connect your experience and interests to the team's actual domain (for example CUDA libraries, AI infrastructure, drivers, or autonomous vehicles). Mention specific NVIDIA technologies you have used or studied and what you want to learn. Show enthusiasm for hard technical problems and the platform approach. Pitfall: talking only about stock price or the AI boom.

looking_for: Whether your interest in this team's domain is real
How your experience connects to the work
strong_signals: Names specific technologies you have used or studied
Links your background to the team's actual domain
Shows enthusiasm for hard technical problems
watch_outs: Talking only about stock price or the AI boom
No knowledge of what the team does

sample_questions.question: Tell me about yourself and walk me through a project on your resume that is closest to this team's work.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Keep the intro short and relevant. For the project, explain the goal, your specific role, the technical design, and measured results. Expect deep technical follow-ups on language, memory, and performance details, so choose a project you can explain at the lowest level. Show how you worked with other teams. Pitfall: a long chronological history.

looking_for: Whether you can pitch yourself briefly and relevantly
How deeply you understand your own project
strong_signals: A short intro that leads to the most relevant project
Explains your role, design and measured results
Holds up under low-level follow-up questions
watch_outs: A long chronological life story
A project you cannot explain in detail

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a product you led from start to finish.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover the problem and customer, how you defined requirements with engineering, the key trade-offs and cuts, launch, and measured results. For NVIDIA, technical credibility matters: show you understood the architecture well enough to make good calls. Include a setback and how you handled it. Pitfall: describing only process and meetings.

looking_for: How you drive a product from idea to launch
Whether you have enough technical depth to make good calls
strong_signals: Covers customer, requirements, trade-offs, launch and results
Shows understanding of the architecture behind decisions
Includes a setback and how you handled it
watch_outs: Describing only process and meetings
No measured outcome

sample_questions.question: What is memory coalescing in CUDA, and why does it matter for performance?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain that threads in a warp access global memory together, and when their addresses fall in contiguous, aligned segments the hardware combines them into few transactions. Uncoalesced access multiplies transactions and wastes bandwidth. Give an example such as row versus column access in a matrix, and fixes like data layout changes (structure of arrays), shared memory tiling, or transposes. Strong answers relate it to achieved versus peak bandwidth and mention profiling to confirm.

looking_for: Whether you understand how GPU memory access works
How you connect concepts to real performance
strong_signals: Explains how a warp's accesses combine into few transactions
Gives an example such as row vs column access
Names fixes like layout changes or shared memory tiling
watch_outs: A definition with no performance impact explained
No mention of profiling to confirm the issue

sample_questions.question: How would you reduce the cost of moving data between host (CPU) memory and device (GPU) memory?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start with why transfers are expensive: interconnect bandwidth is far below device memory bandwidth. Then cover techniques: minimize transfers and keep data on the device, batch small copies, use pinned memory, overlap copies with compute using streams and async copies, and consider unified memory with prefetching. Mention measuring with a profiler and comparing with link bandwidth limits. Pitfall: listing APIs without explaining the reason they help.

looking_for: Whether you know why host-device transfers are costly
How you reduce and hide data movement
strong_signals: Explains the bandwidth gap between interconnect and device memory
Covers batching, pinned memory and overlap with compute
Mentions measuring against link bandwidth limits
watch_outs: Listing APIs without explaining why they help
Ignoring the option of keeping data on the device

sample_questions.question: Explain the difference between kernel mode and user mode, and why the distinction exists.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain privilege levels: kernel mode can execute privileged instructions and access all memory, while user mode is restricted for protection and stability. Describe how user code enters the kernel (system calls, interrupts, exceptions) and the cost of mode switches. Connect it to drivers, which NVIDIA builds, and why moving work to user space can reduce overhead. Clear, accurate layering is the main signal.

looking_for: Whether you understand OS privilege levels
How clearly you explain system layering
strong_signals: Explains what kernel mode allows and why user mode is restricted
Covers system calls, interrupts and mode switch costs
Connects it to drivers and user-space work
watch_outs: Mixing up the layers
No reason given for why the split exists

sample_questions.question: Describe how virtual memory works and what it costs.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover address translation through page tables, the TLB, page faults and demand paging, and protection between processes. Discuss costs: TLB misses, page walks, and faults; mention large pages as a mitigation. A strong answer links to GPUs: unified virtual addressing and page migration between host and device. Pitfall: confusing virtual memory with swap only.

looking_for: Whether you understand address translation
How you reason about the costs of virtual memory
strong_signals: Covers page tables, TLB, page faults and protection
Discusses TLB misses and large pages as a mitigation
Links to unified addressing between host and GPU
watch_outs: Treating virtual memory as just swap
Ignoring performance costs

sample_questions.question: Design a memory allocator, and explain the design choices you would make for performance.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the workload: allocation sizes, threads, and whether it is for CPU or GPU memory. Discuss free lists, size classes, slabs or buddy allocation, fragmentation, and thread-local caches to avoid lock contention. For GPU memory, mention pooling to avoid expensive device allocation calls and stream-ordered reuse. Explain how you would measure fragmentation and latency. Strong answers name trade-offs between speed, memory overhead and fragmentation.

looking_for: How you design for allocation speed and fragmentation
Whether you clarify the workload first
strong_signals: Asks about sizes, threads and CPU vs GPU memory
Covers size classes, free lists and thread-local caches
Names trade-offs and how you would measure them
watch_outs: A single global lock with no thought on contention
No plan to measure fragmentation

sample_questions.question: Design a system for submitting and managing GPU jobs across a shared cluster.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify users, job types (training, inference, batch) and scale. Cover the job API, a queue and scheduler, resource accounting per GPU, priorities and quotas, preemption and checkpointing, placement aware of interconnect topology, and monitoring of utilization and failures. Discuss fairness versus utilization trade-offs and how to handle node failures for long jobs. Pitfall: treating GPUs like generic CPUs and ignoring topology and memory.

looking_for: How you design a shared scheduler for scarce GPUs
Whether you account for GPU-specific constraints
strong_signals: Covers queues, quotas, priorities and preemption
Places jobs with awareness of interconnect topology
Weighs fairness against utilization and handles node failures
watch_outs: Treating GPUs like generic CPUs
No checkpointing for long jobs

sample_questions.question: Explain what a mixture-of-experts model is and why it changes the compute and memory picture compared to a dense model.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain that a router sends each token to a small subset of expert sub-networks, so compute per token stays low while total parameters grow. Discuss consequences: memory to hold all experts, load balancing across experts, communication when experts sit on different GPUs, and batching inefficiency. Compare briefly with dense models. Strong answers also mention how this affects inference serving. Pitfall: vague description with no systems implications.

looking_for: Whether you understand sparse model architectures
How you reason about compute and memory trade-offs
strong_signals: Explains routing tokens to a few experts
Covers memory, load balancing and cross-GPU communication
Mentions effects on inference serving
watch_outs: A vague description with no systems implications
Confusing compute per token with total parameters

sample_questions.question: How would you explain the use of GPUs for deep learning to a business stakeholder?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain that deep learning is dominated by large matrix operations that can be split into many independent pieces, which GPUs run in parallel across thousands of cores with high memory bandwidth. Mention the software stack (CUDA and libraries) that makes this usable. Tie it to business outcomes like training time and inference cost. Keep it simple and accurate. Pitfall: jargon without a clear causal chain.

looking_for: Whether you can explain a technical idea to a non-expert
How accurate you stay while simplifying
strong_signals: A clear causal chain from parallel math to GPUs
Mentions the software stack that makes it usable
Ties it to business outcomes like training time and cost
watch_outs: Jargon with no clear explanation
Oversimplifying until it is wrong

sample_questions.question: How would you improve the user experience of GeForce NOW?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define the users (gamers on low-end devices, travelers, and so on) and their main pains, such as latency, queue times, game library and price. Pick one segment and problem, propose solutions, and prioritize by impact and feasibility given infrastructure costs. Define metrics like session length, retention and conversion to paid tiers, plus guardrails like latency. Pitfall: ignoring the cost of server capacity.

looking_for: How you pick a user segment and their main pain
Whether you weigh solutions against infrastructure cost
strong_signals: Defines users and picks one segment and problem
Prioritizes by impact and feasibility
Defines metrics with guardrails such as latency
watch_outs: Ignoring server capacity costs
Features with no target user

sample_questions.question: What new market could NVIDIA's AI technology expand into, and how would you evaluate it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Generate a few candidate markets, then evaluate with clear criteria: market size (with a rough estimate and assumptions), fit with NVIDIA's platform strengths, competition, and time to revenue. Pick one and recommend a first step such as a partnership, SDK, or reference design. Address risks. NVIDIA thinks in platforms and ecosystems, so mention developers. Pitfall: picking a market without sizing it.

looking_for: How you generate and evaluate new markets
Whether you think in platforms and ecosystems
strong_signals: Compares candidates on size, fit, competition and time to revenue
Gives a rough size with stated assumptions
Recommends a concrete first step and addresses risks
watch_outs: Picking a market without sizing it
Forgetting developers and partners

sample_questions.question: Sales of one of your products are declining. How would you investigate?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the size and timing of the drop, then segment: region, channel, customer type, product SKU. Check external factors (competitor launch, seasonality, supply constraints, a new generation announced) and internal ones (price changes, quality issues). Form hypotheses, say what data confirms each, and recommend actions. Pitfall: jumping to a single cause.

looking_for: How you structure an investigation into declining sales
Whether you consider both internal and external causes
strong_signals: Clarifies the size and timing of the drop
Segments by region, channel, customer and product
Names data to confirm each hypothesis, then actions
watch_outs: Jumping to a single cause
No segmentation before forming conclusions

sample_questions.question: You can fund either a user-facing feature or stability and performance work this quarter. How do you choose?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Lay out a framework: customer impact, revenue or retention risk, effort, and strategic importance. Quantify where possible, for example crash rates or support costs versus expected adoption of the feature. Consider options like partial scope. Make a clear recommendation and explain how you would communicate it. Pitfall: refusing to choose.

looking_for: How you prioritize between competing investments
Whether you make a clear call and explain it
strong_signals: Uses a framework of customer impact, risk, effort and strategy
Quantifies where possible
Considers partial scope and how to communicate the decision
watch_outs: Refusing to choose
Deciding on gut feel alone

sample_questions.question: Walk me through autoregressive decoding in an LLM. What does the KV cache store, and what does it cost?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain that the model generates one token at a time, and each step attends to all earlier tokens. The KV cache keeps the key and value tensors of past tokens per layer and head, so each step only computes projections for the new token. Size it: layers x heads x head dimension x sequence length x batch x 2 x bytes per element. Then name the costs: memory grows with context and batch, decode becomes memory-bandwidth bound, and fragmentation limits batch size. Mention fixes such as paged allocation, grouped-query attention, and quantized caches.

looking_for: Whether you understand token-by-token generation
Whether you can size the cache and name its bottleneck
strong_signals: Explains what is cached and why it avoids recomputation
Gives a size formula and a rough number
Says decode is memory-bandwidth bound and names fixes
watch_outs: Describing the cache without its memory cost
Ignoring batch size and context length

sample_questions.question: Explain beam search for LLM inference and the time and memory cost of each step.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe keeping the k best partial sequences, expanding each with the next-token distribution, scoring by summed log probability (often length-normalized), and keeping the top k. Give the cost per step: k forward passes or one batched pass, a top-k over k x vocabulary candidates, and k copies of the KV cache, which can share prefixes. Compare with greedy and sampling, and say when beam search helps (translation) or hurts (open-ended chat). Strong answers mention batching the beams on the GPU.

looking_for: Whether you know how beam search works step by step
How you reason about its cost on a GPU
strong_signals: Explains expansion, scoring and pruning to k beams
Gives per-step compute and KV cache cost
Compares with greedy decoding and sampling
watch_outs: No complexity analysis
Forgetting the extra KV cache memory per beam

sample_questions.question: What is LoRA, and why does it make fine-tuning a large model cheaper?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain that LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and learns a low-rank update for chosen layers: two small matrices whose product has the shape of the original weight. Only those small matrices get gradients and optimizer state, so training memory and checkpoint size drop sharply. Discuss the choice of rank and target layers, merging the update into the weights for inference at no extra latency, and serving many adapters on one base model. Mention limits: lower capacity than full fine-tuning for large domain shifts.

looking_for: Whether you understand parameter-efficient fine-tuning
How you connect the method to memory and serving costs
strong_signals: Explains the frozen base and low-rank update
Says where the memory savings come from
Mentions merging and multi-adapter serving
watch_outs: Only reciting the acronym
Claiming it is always as good as full fine-tuning

sample_questions.question: Compare quantization approaches for inference. When would you choose each?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover post-training quantization (weight-only or weights and activations, INT8, FP8 or 4-bit) versus quantization-aware training. Explain the trade-offs: memory and bandwidth savings, speedups only when the hardware has fast kernels for that format, and accuracy loss from outliers in activations. Mention calibration data, per-channel or per-group scales, and keeping sensitive layers at higher precision. Say how you would validate: accuracy on a task suite plus measured latency and throughput.

looking_for: Whether you know the main quantization options
How you weigh accuracy against speed and memory
strong_signals: Contrasts post-training and quantization-aware training
Ties speedups to hardware support for the format
Validates with both accuracy and measured performance
watch_outs: Assuming lower precision is always faster
No plan to check accuracy

sample_questions.question: Design an inference serving system for a large model that must handle about 10,000 requests per second.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start with targets: latency per request (time to first token and per token), throughput, model size and traffic shape. Then cover the request path, a router and load balancer, dynamic or continuous batching, model replicas and how the model is split across GPUs, KV cache management, autoscaling and admission control. Estimate GPUs needed from measured tokens per second per GPU. Discuss trade-offs between batch size and latency, and monitoring of GPU utilization and tail latency.

looking_for: How you design for a throughput and latency target
Whether you size the system with numbers
strong_signals: Clarifies latency, throughput and model size first
Uses dynamic batching and explains its latency cost
Estimates GPU count from per-GPU throughput
watch_outs: Generic web-service design with no GPU specifics
No numbers behind the capacity plan

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to bridge the gap between research and engineering.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a case where a research result had to become production code or a product feature. Explain what was hard: reproducibility, performance, scale or different priorities. Show your own actions, such as building a benchmark both sides trusted, simplifying the method, or setting a shared definition of done. Quantify the result, for example speedup or accuracy kept. NVIDIA values one team across research and engineering, so show shared credit. Pitfall: blaming the other side.

looking_for: How you turn research into working systems
Whether you work well across research and engineering
strong_signals: Names the concrete gap, such as speed or reproducibility
Shows your own actions and a shared measure of success
Quantifies the outcome
watch_outs: Blaming researchers or engineers
No measurable result

sample_questions.question: How would you build the schedule for a program where new hardware and its software stack are developed at the same time?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Lay out the hardware milestones (architecture, tape-out, first silicon, bring-up, production) and map software work to each: work on simulators and emulation before silicon, then bring-up and validation. Identify the critical path and dependencies in both directions, add buffers where hardware dates are uncertain, and define exit criteria per milestone. Explain how you track risk and what you would cut or move if silicon slips. Close with how you report status to leadership.

looking_for: Whether you understand hardware and software milestones
How you manage dependencies and schedule risk
strong_signals: Maps software work to pre-silicon and post-silicon phases
Names the critical path and where buffers go
Has a plan for a silicon slip
watch_outs: Treating it like a pure software release
No exit criteria for milestones

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time a program you ran was at risk of missing a critical milestone.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the program, the milestone and why it mattered. Explain how you spotted the risk early (metrics, dependency tracking), what options you laid out, the trade-off you drove, and how you told stakeholders, including bad news. Give the result in dates or scope and what you changed in your process. NVIDIA prizes intellectual honesty, so raise risk early and plainly. Pitfall: a story where you only reported status and others solved it.

looking_for: How early you detect and raise risk
How you drive trade-offs to recover
strong_signals: Shows the early warning signal you used
Lays out options and the trade-off chosen
Reports bad news openly and on time
watch_outs: Only reporting status while others acted
Hiding the risk until it was too late

sample_questions.question: Describe a decision you made that was not well received. How did you build buy-in afterwards?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain the decision, why you made it and who disagreed. Show you listened to the objections, shared the data and reasoning openly, and changed parts of the plan where the critics were right. Describe concrete steps such as a review with affected teams or a checkpoint to revisit. End with the outcome and the relationships. Pitfall: forcing the decision through on authority alone.

looking_for: How you handle pushback on your decisions
Whether you build alignment instead of forcing it
strong_signals: Listens to objections and shares the reasoning
Adjusts where the critics were right
Ends with the outcome and the relationship
watch_outs: Relying on authority alone
Dismissing the people who disagreed

sample_questions.question: Walk me through a large program you ran end to end. Which KPIs did you use to judge its success?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give the goal, scope, teams involved and your role. Name a few KPIs tied to outcomes (delivery dates met, quality, adoption, performance) plus leading indicators you tracked weekly. Explain how a KPI changed a decision during the program. Close with the measured result and what you would change. Pitfall: listing activity metrics like meetings held or tickets closed.

looking_for: The scale of programs you have run
Whether you measure outcomes, not activity
strong_signals: Clear scope, teams and your own role
Outcome KPIs plus leading indicators
A decision the data changed
watch_outs: Activity metrics only
No measured result

sample_questions.question: Compare NVLink and InfiniBand. When does each matter for a customer's AI cluster?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain that NVLink connects GPUs within a node (or a rack-scale domain) with very high bandwidth, used for tensor and pipeline parallel traffic, while InfiniBand (or high-speed Ethernet) connects nodes across the cluster for data-parallel gradient exchange and storage. Discuss bandwidth and latency differences, topology, and how the parallelism strategy decides which link is the bottleneck. Tie it to sizing a customer cluster and to collective communication libraries.

looking_for: Whether you understand GPU cluster networking
How you match interconnects to workloads
strong_signals: Separates scale-up inside a node from scale-out across nodes
Links each parallelism type to the network it stresses
Ties the answer to a customer sizing decision
watch_outs: Treating the two as interchangeable
No link to the customer's workload

sample_questions.question: A customer says their GPUs are badly underused during training. How would you troubleshoot it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start by measuring: GPU utilization over time, memory use, and a profiler timeline. Check the usual causes in order: the input pipeline (data loading, preprocessing on CPU, storage throughput), small batch sizes, host-device copies, communication stalls between GPUs or nodes, and kernels with low occupancy or no mixed precision. Propose a fix for each finding and verify with numbers. Explain how you would report results to the customer clearly.

looking_for: How you diagnose performance problems systematically
Whether you measure before fixing
strong_signals: Starts with profiling data, not guesses
Checks input pipeline, batch size, copies and communication
Verifies each fix with numbers
watch_outs: Jumping straight to buying more hardware
A list of causes with no order or method

sample_questions.question: Design data center infrastructure for a customer who wants to train large language models.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the model sizes, training timeline, budget, and whether they also need inference. Estimate compute from model size and tokens, then the GPU count for the timeline. Cover node choice, intra-node and inter-node networking, storage throughput for data and checkpoints, power and cooling, and the software stack and scheduler. Discuss build versus cloud options and phased rollout. Recommend one design with its risks.

looking_for: How you turn customer needs into a system design
Whether you size compute with clear assumptions
strong_signals: Clarifies goals, timeline and budget first
Estimates GPU count from compute needed
Covers network, storage, power and software, then recommends
watch_outs: Listing products with no sizing
Ignoring storage, power or operations

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to say no to a customer request.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the request, why it was not right (technical limits, cost, roadmap or risk to the customer), and how you said no with data and an alternative. Show that you kept the relationship and, if relevant, passed the need to the product team. End with what happened to the customer's goal. Pitfall: saying no without explaining or offering a path.

looking_for: Whether you can be honest with customers
How you protect the relationship while saying no
strong_signals: Explains the reason with data
Offers an alternative path
Passes the need on to the product team
watch_outs: A flat no with no explanation
Saying yes to everything

sample_questions.question: How would you prioritize features for the next generation of a GPU product?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Segment customers, such as cloud providers, enterprises, researchers, gamers and developers, and name the workloads each cares about. Translate those into needs: compute, memory capacity and bandwidth, power, interconnect, and software support. Weigh each candidate feature by customer value, competitive position, cost and schedule risk. Make a clear call and say what you would give up. Strong answers treat the software ecosystem as part of the product.

looking_for: How you connect customer workloads to hardware features
Whether you make a clear prioritization call
strong_signals: Segments customers and their workloads
Weighs value, competition, cost and schedule risk
Treats software support as part of the product
watch_outs: Picking specs with no customer link
Refusing to trade anything off

sample_questions.question: How would you measure success for an AI developer platform?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define the platform's goal and its users first. Build a metric chain: reach (sign-ups, downloads), activation (time to first working result), engagement and retention (weekly active developers, projects in production), and business impact (paid usage, GPU demand it drives). Pick one primary metric, add guardrails such as performance and support load, and say how you would break metrics down by segment. Pitfall: counting downloads only.

looking_for: How you choose metrics tied to the platform's goal
Whether you think about developers as users
strong_signals: Builds a chain from reach to activation to retention to business
Picks a primary metric and guardrails
Segments metrics by user type
watch_outs: Vanity metrics such as downloads only
No link to business outcomes

sample_questions.question: One of your product lines is losing market share. What do you do?
sample_questions.strong_answer: First confirm the size and where the loss is: segments, regions, price points. Look for causes outside (a competitor's new product, price changes, a market shift) and inside (performance gaps, supply, software issues, pricing). Form hypotheses and the data to test each. Then propose responses with trade-offs, such as pricing, a software update, repositioning or speeding up the next product, and recommend one with success metrics. Pitfall: cutting price as the only answer.

looking_for: How you diagnose a competitive decline
Whether you recommend a response with trade-offs
strong_signals: Locates the loss before explaining it
Considers outside and inside causes
Recommends one response with metrics
watch_outs: Price cuts as the only lever
No data to test the hypotheses

sample_questions.question: Explain how a cache coherence protocol such as MESI keeps multiple cores' caches consistent.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name the four states (Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid) and walk through transitions: a read miss, a write to a shared line that invalidates other copies, and a write-back on eviction of a modified line. Explain snooping versus directory-based approaches and why directories scale better. Discuss the performance costs: coherence traffic and false sharing, with how to avoid it through data layout. Clear state diagrams and a concrete example are the main signal.

looking_for: Whether you understand cache coherence
How clearly you explain state transitions
strong_signals: Names the states and walks through key transitions
Contrasts snooping and directory protocols
Explains false sharing and how to avoid it
watch_outs: Listing states without transitions
No link to performance

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: New college grad (posting pay band 'Level 1'; a BS or MS, sometimes a PhD, and no years required). Works on defined tasks with review from a more senior engineer and ramps up quickly on the hardware and CUDA.

Engineer with about 2 to 5 years (posting band 'Level 2'; untitled 'System Software Engineer' postings ask for 3+ years). Owns small features end to end with light review; work is still scoped by others.

Senior engineer (posting band 'Level 3'; Senior postings ask for 3 to 5+ years). Owns a component, drives complex work across teams without close supervision, reviews code and debugs across module boundaries.

Senior engineer at the upper band (posting band 'Level 4'; some Senior postings ask for 8 to 10+ years). Sets the plan for an area, writes architecture specs, and carries projects that depend on two or more teams, often across hardware and software.
Senior staff or tech lead (posting band 'Level 5'). Owns a large product area and sets its technical direction; other teams consult them before building.

Principal engineer (Principal postings ask for about 12+ years). Sets technical direction across several teams or a whole area of NVIDIA software, such as a compiler stack or inference runtime, and settles the hardest technical disagreements.

Distinguished engineer (postings ask for 15 to 18+ years). Defines multi-generation strategy across hardware, software and systems, aligns architects from many teams on shared metrics, presents to senior technical and business leaders, and mentors senior engineers.
Owns model training or inference work for a product area, tunes performance on NVIDIA GPUs, and works with research and product teams.

About 12+ years. Leads model performance or algorithm direction across architectures and accelerator types, contributes to public frameworks such as TensorRT, and partners with several product groups.
Often 8 to 10+ years. Runs several concurrent cross-functional programs, aligns software with hardware timelines, builds risk metrics, and reports status to executives.
Postings use pay bands Level 4 and 5. Owns a product or platform area, works deep in engineering trade-offs, and drives go-to-market with sales and partners.
Leads technical engagements with major customers, designs GPU infrastructure and AI solutions, and feeds customer needs back to product teams.

persona.tone: Technical, direct and conversational; a future teammate talking shop rather than reading from a script
persona.pace: Fast; checks fundamentals early, then drills quickly into low-level detail of the candidate's own projects
persona.pushback_style: Asks 'how close is that to the theoretical limit?', 'what does the hardware actually do?' and 'how did you measure it?'; challenges hand-wavy answers, removes shortcuts (no library call, no built-in), and gives a hint if the candidate is stuck and says so
persona.closing_style: Leaves about 5 to 10 minutes for questions about the team's technical work; no feedback given in the room

case_style.notes: PM cases are product strategy and prioritization for NVIDIA platforms (GPUs, developer platforms, cloud gaming), go-to-market and competitive positioning, always tied to hardware/software trade-offs. Market sizing appears in one guide only. Some loops use a prepared case presentation. TPM cases are programs at risk and hardware/software schedules; solutions architect cases are customer AI infrastructure designs.

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: the Code of Conduct PDF is still too large for our fetcher (over 10 MB); the five value names are confirmed by the PDF's search snippet and several secondary pages, and descriptions are paraphrased from those. The value weights are our estimate.

loop_structure: NVIDIA's official page confirms phone interviews, 30-60 minute panels, HackerRank coding and a required onsite, but each team runs its own loop; round lists per role family are typical patterns from prep guides and candidate reports.

loop_structure: the solutions architect loop is the only 'other' family modeled; ASIC and hardware design loops are mostly RTL, SystemVerilog and coding and are not simulated. The data_ml, tpm and solutions architect loops each rest on one or two prep guides plus candidate reports.

bar_by_level: NVIDIA publishes no ladder. The IC labels come from one third-party source; official job postings (read through job-board mirrors, because the Workday site renders no text for our fetcher) confirm 'Level 1' to 'Level 5' pay bands and the years asked for Senior, Principal and Distinguished titles. Data_ml, tpm, pm and solutions architect scopes are our summaries of single postings.
persona: drawn from prep guides and candidate reports that agree on conversational, detail-drilling interviewers; NVIDIA publishes no description of interviewer style.

scoring_weights: derived from what official job postings consistently require (deep C/C++ and architecture skills, collaboration and influence across groups) and from the stated values; no public source gives competency weights, so the numbers are our estimate.
case_style: PM case mix now rests on three prep guides that agree on product strategy plus hardware/software trade-offs; only one mentions market sizing, so estimation is weighted low.
